group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 65-year-old woman with a decade-long history of systolic pump dysfunction treated in the community with carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, and a home loop diuretic regimen was brought to the emergency department by her adult son after he found her sitting at the kitchen table early this morning staring at an untouched cup of coffee, repeatedly asking what day it was and why the lights were on; he noted that she had been coughing “rust-colored gunk” for the past two days and had complained last night that lying flat made her breathing harder, though she denied chest pressure at that time. She normally ambulates short city blocks with a cane, keeps meticulous pillboxes, and manages online banking without assistance; the abrupt disorientation frightened the family, who immediately called emergency medical services. Prehospital personnel documented labored breathing but no cyanosis and elected not to initiate oxygen so that baseline gases could be obtained on arrival. The patient denies recent fevers until yesterday evening when she recorded an ear temperature “a little over 102 °F,” and she recalls a single episode of chills that resolved spontaneously. She has never been told of chronic kidney trouble, treated liver illness, or any kind of malignancy, and her last outpatient basic metabolic panel one month earlier was unremarkable aside from marginal hyponatremia related to diuretic use that required only routine surveillance. She quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks wine only on major holidays, and uses no illicit substances. She last received influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations during last winter’s cardiology follow-up. At triage, before any antipyretics, antibiotics, diuretics, or supplemental oxygen were administered, her oral temperature registered 38.9 °C, radial pulse 111 beats per minute in a regular rhythm, automated blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute with shallow accessory muscle use, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuated between 87 – 88 % on ambient air. The patient was awake but intermittently inattentive, oriented to name only, and scored 14 on the Glasgow Coma Scale owing to temporal disorientation and slowed responses. Skin was warm and perfused, with no mottling; neck veins were not distended at 45°, and there was no peripheral edema. Cardiac examination revealed a rapid S1 and S2 with a soft holosystolic murmur at the apex consistent with her known functional regurgitation but no new gallops or rubs. Lung auscultation detected coarse inspiratory crackles over the right mid-lung field and markedly diminished breath sounds at the right costophrenic recess with stony dullness to percussion, whereas the left side had scattered late crackles at the base without wheeze. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and nondistended, bowel sounds normoactive, and no hepatosplenomegaly was appreciated. Finger-stick capillary glucose measured 122 mg/dL. Blood drawn within fifteen minutes of arrival, prior to any intravenous fluid, revealed hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL with hematocrit 49 %, white blood cell count 14.1 × 10⁹/L (84 % neutrophils), platelet count 172 × 10⁹/L, sodium 147 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 108 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (baseline), and high-sensitivity troponin T below assay detection. An arterial blood gas obtained while she remained on room air demonstrated pH 7.43, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, PaO₂ 66 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, with lactate 1.5 mmol/L from a concurrent venous sample. Upright posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiographs showed a dense consolidation occupying the right lower lobe with a large meniscus of fluid layering laterally and blunting of the right costophrenic angle, while the cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from imaging five months earlier; the left lung fields were clear except for subtle interstitial markings at the base. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia at 112 bpm with nonspecific ST-T wave changes but no acute ischemia or conduction delay. Bedside lung ultrasound corroborated an anechoic stripe measuring up to 2.5 cm over the right hemidiaphragm with dynamic air bronchograms in the consolidated parenchyma, and B-lines were sparse on the contralateral side. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a viral respiratory panel were obtained before any medication administration; no intravenous lines other than heparinized saline locks had been flushed, and no diuretic dose was given in the emergency department up to the point of this documentation so that initial laboratory values accurately represent her untreated state.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
• Demographics: woman aged 65 → 65 − 10 = 55. No nursing-home residence: 0.
• Comorbidities: chronic heart failure adds 10. No reported neoplastic, liver, cerebrovascular, or renal disease: 0 each.
• Examination: new disorientation adds 20; respiratory rate 32/min (≥30) adds 20. Systolic BP 108 (not <90), temperature 38.9 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 111/min (<125): 0 each.
• Laboratory data: pH 7.43 (not <7.35), BUN 19 mg/dL (<30), sodium 147 mEq/L (not <130), glucose 122 mg/dL (<250), and hematocrit 49% (not <30%): 0 each. Using the measured room-air PaO₂ of 66 mm Hg, the PaO₂ <60 criterion scores 0.
• Pleural effusion on chest radiograph adds 10.
Total = 55 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 115 (risk class IV).
Final answer: 115
